summaries.headline: New Mexico Districts Reject State's AI Reading Tool
summaries.summary: Santa Fe and Los Alamos public schools are refusing to deploy Amira, a state-mandated AI reading assessment, when classes resume this fall, citing unresolved student data privacy concerns. The software listens to students read aloud and flags errors, but parents worry their children's voice recordings are being used to train commercial AI products without adequate safeguards. Santa Fe Superintendent Christine Griffin said the district will pause the tool, including its voice-recording feature, until the state education department provides clearer guidance—a standoff that signals growing friction between state ed-tech mandates and local data-privacy accountability.

summaries.headline: Colorado District Adopts Texas Bible-Infused Curriculum
summaries.summary: Montezuma-Cortez, a 2,200-student district in southwestern Colorado, bypassed more than 20 state-approved reading options this summer to adopt Bluebonnet, a Texas-designed elementary curriculum that weaves Biblical content into lessons, including Genesis creation stories for kindergartners and the Parable of the Prodigal Son for first graders. The pick came with little public discussion or school board vote, and stems from the district's adoption of Houston Superintendent Mike Miles's "New Education System" reform model, which Houston paired with Bluebonnet this summer; Colorado's local-control rules only require non-state-approved curricula to be evidence-based, not publicly vetted. A low-performing district importing a religiously infused, unvetted curriculum designed for another state's students raises questions that will likely extend well beyond Montezuma-Cortez's borders.

summaries.headline: Federal Funding Uncertainty Clouds 2026-27 School Budgets
summaries.summary: District leaders are heading into the 2026-27 budget cycle with more open questions than answers, as a newly created federal education tax credit and unresolved congressional budget negotiations leave key funding streams in limbo. Education Week's outlook flags these as the two variables most likely to reshape district revenue projections in the coming year, though specifics on dollar amounts and implementation timelines remain unsettled at the federal level. Business officials and superintendents building next year's budgets will need to plan for volatility rather than certainty until Washington finalizes its numbers.

summaries.headline: Federal Funding Turmoil Compounds State-Level Fiscal Strain
summaries.summary: Federal dollars make up roughly 1 in every 10 dollars spent on K-12 schools, but the second Trump administration's aggressive moves have made even that modest share unpredictable for district budgets. In under two years, the administration has canceled hundreds of grants and contracts worth billions, dismantled agencies, delayed formula fund payments, and frozen research spending—actions Education Week notes have at times appeared to defy law and the Constitution. District leaders now face this federal instability layered on top of already precarious state and local funding structures, leaving budget planning a far riskier exercise than in past years.

summaries.headline: Senate Panel Advances Two Reading Bills
summaries.summary: A Senate committee cleared two bills Thursday that would deepen federal involvement in how schools teach reading, reflecting Congress' sustained attention to the "science of reading" movement. The bipartisan READ Act would tighten requirements on existing federal literacy grants, mandating early screening for reading difficulties and evidence-based instruction while redirecting funding toward states with the weakest reading scores; the companion 21st Century Dyslexia Act would carve out dyslexia as its own category under federal disability law rather than folding it into broader classifications. With only 1 in 3 students leaving high school as proficient readers, according to sponsor Sen. Maggie Hassan, the legislation signals that literacy screening and instructional practice may soon face more direct federal scrutiny, regardless of where the bills ultimately land.

summaries.summary: The provided source material contains only website navigation elements and category menus from District Administration's site, with no actual article text about chronic absenteeism reversal strategies. Without the substantive content—including which districts are cited, what interventions they used, or what data supports the "reversal" claim—an accurate, non-fabricated summary cannot be produced. Please provide the full article text or a working link to the piece so the newsletter entry reflects the actual reporting.

summaries.headline: Teacher Shortage Is Real, Unevenly Distributed
summaries.summary: A former Chicago assistant principal argues the national debate over teacher shortages misses the point by focusing on aggregate supply-and-demand numbers that look balanced on paper. He recalls physics postings once drawing 20 applicants and English postings drawing 150 in the late 1990s, compared to just one or two qualified candidates by the time he left the district, with recent layoffs driven by enrollment declines, expiring pandemic funds, and budget cuts rather than a genuine surplus of qualified teachers. The mismatch between national statistics and building-level reality means shortages concentrate in specific subjects, schools, and communities — leaving the students in those classrooms to absorb the consequences of a debate about whether the problem exists at all.

summaries.headline: Chicago School Board Bets Big on Unproven State Funds
summaries.summary: Chicago's school board passed a nearly $10 billion budget that reverses planned layoffs but leans on $150 million in additional state funding that hasn't been approved and may never come. CPS CEO Macquline King warned parents the district might not secure short-term financing to cover September payroll, raising the specter of a delayed school start on Aug. 24, though financial experts say a high-interest loan would likely avert that outcome. With every school board seat up for election in November and state lawmakers unlikely to revisit an already-finalized budget, this fiscal gamble sets up a fight that could define the district's governance fight for months to come.

summaries.headline: AI Slop Surfaces on Teachers Pay Teachers
summaries.summary: Teachers Pay Teachers, used by 85% of pre-K-12 educators in the U.S., is facing scrutiny after a Chalkbeat review found AI-generated resources riddled with factual errors and bizarre imagery for sale on the platform. Examples include a Black history poster mislabeling George Crum's potato chip invention with an image of a firefighter, an alphabet worksheet missing the letter F, and a presidents poster illustrating Martin Van Buren's resilience with an asteroid striking anti-slavery demonstrators. The platform's namesake premise — teachers vetting content for other teachers — is central to its credibility, and unchecked AI-generated material slipping through that system raises the stakes for what ends up in front of students.

summaries.headline: Harvard Tests How AI Toys Reshape Kids' Play
summaries.summary: Harvard Graduate School of Education researchers have built their own AI-enabled toy and started lab testing to examine how it affects children's language development, imagination, social behavior, trust and attachment compared with traditional toys, with a longitudinal home-based phase planned next. Unlike a conventional teddy bear that stays silent until a child assigns it a voice, an AI toy can remember past conversations, introduce its own topics, and steer play, raising what researchers call a "redistribution of agency" between child and system. As AI toys reach more households, school leaders and early-childhood educators may soon face questions about their classroom presence and developmental impact well before conclusive research exists.

summaries.headline: Missouri Funding Decision Hits District Budgets Hard
summaries.summary: Missouri's state budget decisions are creating significant shortfalls for local school districts. Ritenour School District's superintendent reports the funding outcome translates to a $3.5 million hit to their budget. Districts across the state now face the task of absorbing multimillion-dollar gaps without clear guidance on where those cuts will land.

summaries.headline: New Jersey Launches Overhaul of School Funding Formula
summaries.summary: The Sherrill administration and New Jersey Department of Education have launched a statewide outreach effort to review and potentially rework the state's school funding formula, responding to complaints from educators and families that current funding falls short despite record education spending. The initiative includes an online learning series explaining how state aid is calculated, stakeholder engagement sessions, and a steering committee — led by Commissioner Lily Laux and supported by the nonpartisan Hunt Institute — that will begin meeting this fall to study national best practices and recommend reforms. Feedback gathered this year will inform recommendations to the Legislature, with the broader reform conversation expected to continue through 2027, giving districts a multi-year window to watch how funding stability, transparency and cost pressures get addressed at the state level.

summaries.headline: NYC Mandates School Avoidance Liaisons in Every School
summaries.summary: New York City's Education Department has agreed to overhaul how it handles chronic absenteeism tied to school avoidance, settling with attorneys who sued in October 2024 on behalf of four students with disabilities who stopped attending school regularly. The agreement, signed after more than a year of negotiation, requires every school across the five boroughs to designate a school avoidance liaison and mandates systemwide training aimed at identifying root causes like anxiety and depression rather than treating absences as simple refusal. The case survived even after a judge dismissed the underlying lawsuit, signaling that the city saw enough merit in the claims to commit to policy changes rather than fight the appeal.

summaries.headline: Philadelphia Parents Push City to End Preschool Pushout
summaries.summary: Philadelphia parents told City Council this week that preschool suspensions and informal exclusions have derailed their young children's learning, with one mother describing being told her autistic son could no longer attend after his very first day. The practice, often called "preschool pushout," is notoriously hard to track since many exclusions go undocumented, but the city already bars any city-funded pre-K program — including the roughly 5,000 PHLpreK seats — from removing children or sending them home early, a rule officials admit providers have struggled to follow. Parents and advocates are now demanding an outright ban on preschool exclusion citywide along with deeper investment in early childhood training and disability support, putting pressure on both the city and school district to close the gap between policy and practice.

summaries.headline: Data Centers Are Creeping Up on Schools
summaries.summary: Nearly 1,900 U.S. public schools now sit within a mile of a data center, as AI-driven demand for computing infrastructure pushes new construction into residential and rural areas once considered off-limits. In Coweta County, Georgia, families near 70-year-old Arnco-Sargent Elementary are fighting a proposed decade-long data center project on 832 rezoned acres, citing traffic, noise, and water-quality concerns, while research cited in the analysis links proximity to these facilities with lower student math scores. As tech companies race to site infrastructure near power and fiber lines, district leaders and local officials are increasingly the last line of defense for communities weighing economic development against classroom conditions.

summaries.headline: Private Dollars Fund Oklahoma's Literacy Coach Push
summaries.summary: Oklahoma's State Chamber of Commerce is directing $1.5 million in private donations from the Walton Family Foundation, Choctaw Nation, and Emerson Collective to train literacy coaches in 10 schools across seven traditional districts, two charter schools, and one neighborhood school. The pilot, which began training coaches in July on the "science of reading," is designed to get ahead of the Strong Readers Act, a law taking effect in 2027-28 that will hold back third graders who read below basic grade level and mandates more literacy coaches statewide. State Chamber leaders are explicitly modeling the effort on Mississippi's reading reforms, where a $100 million private donation is widely credited alongside legislation for that state's decade-long climb in national rankings, betting that private capital can move faster than the $5 million lawmakers allocated this year for state-run coaching expansion.

summaries.headline: Little Rock Schools Post Literacy Gains, Launch New Programs
summaries.summary: Little Rock School District enters the new school year touting measurable literacy gains alongside a slate of new initiatives, including a bilingual program and Hall High School's transition to charter status. District leaders are positioning these moves as evidence of academic momentum heading into the fall semester. The pairing of instructional gains with structural changes like the charter conversion signals a district testing multiple levers—curriculum and governance—to sustain improvement.

summaries.headline: Randolph Schools Push to Lock Down Vendor Data Deals
summaries.summary: The Randolph Board of Education accepted member Hazel Ball's resignation and opened a window for candidates to apply for her seat, with interviews set for August 27 and filings due August 14. Director of Technology Peter Emmel told the board that more than 75% of the district's technology vendors now have signed data privacy agreements in place, with a goal of closing the gap with remaining vendors before the 2026-27 school year begins. As districts increasingly outsource instructional tools and services, vendor-level data agreements are becoming as central to student privacy protection as internal IT policy.

summaries.headline: Bipartisan Bill Ties Federal Dollars to Science of Reading
summaries.summary: Sens. Ted Cruz and Brian Schatz introduced the Improving America's Literacy Act, which would direct federal education funding toward instruction grounded in the five pillars of the Science of Reading—phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency and comprehension—without altering how states allocate their own education dollars. The push comes as spending has climbed 56% since 2013 to roughly $16,700 per student nationally while math and reading scores have dropped 12 and six points respectively, and as Texas's $454 million literacy grant works out to just $82 per student against a backdrop of $8,500-$9,000 in standard per-pupil operating funds. The bill would also task the Institute of Education Sciences with auditing state literacy and numeracy strategies, signaling that future federal support may hinge less on how much states spend and more on whether their instructional materials actually align with reading research.

# Alachua County Reads Collaborative Literacy Initiative Takes Big Steps Forward

**Published on 8/6/2026**

**by**

Last updated: 8/6/2026 4:30 PM

Page Content

​ _**This news release is being published at the request of Alachua County Reads.**_

The Alachua County Reads (ACR) collaborative continues its countywide effort to improve literacy for residents of all ages. The Virtual Literacy Hub at [www.alachuacountyreads.org](https://alachuacounty.us/News/Article/Pages/Alachua-County-Reads-Collaborative-Literacy-Initiative-Takes-Big-Steps-Forward.aspx#) launched on Aug. 1, 2026, and programming across community-based partners and the Alachua County Public Schools is expanding to meet intervention and instructional support priorities.

The ACR initiative traces back to April 2025, when the Alachua County Commission, the Children's Trust of Alachua County and Alachua County Public Schools released the Alachua County Comprehensive Literacy Needs Assessment (ACCLNA), completed by the Lastinger Center at the University of Florida.

The assessment identified the key activities and priorities needed to improve literacy rates for residents of all ages, from early childhood through adulthood, by coordinating efforts to expand school readiness, support training for Alachua County Public Schools (ACPS) teachers in K-2 classrooms, and build up intervention programs for children, youth, and adults who need to improve their reading skills. ACR begins with a three-year investment to build the activities and collaboration needed to achieve the long-term goals identified in the assessment.

“The ACR initiative is a concerted, collective and collaborative community effort to meet the literacy needs of our children and adults to improve life outcomes,” said Alachua County Reads Project Coordinator Heidi Keegan. “This project aims to help our citizens thrive and create the economic and social opportunities they deserve.”

The ACR collaborative began meeting in May 2025 to identify partners and outline action items to meet the priorities of the assessment and achieve the following comprehensive community goals:

- Strengthen kindergarten readiness through high-quality VPK
- Help students read on grade level by the end of third grade
- Provide extra literacy support for students who need it most
- Expand adult literacy opportunities

Phase 1 was funded through an $800,000 investment from the Alachua County Commission and the Children's Trust of Alachua County. In October 2025, Alachua County launched its Literacy Catalyst Initiative, operated by PEAK Literacy, which provides high-dosage reading tutoring to more than 300 youth across 11 participating community organizations using the Great Leaps Reading Intervention. The initiative also plans to expand adult literacy services.

ACR serves as the coordination lead, bringing partners together, engaging experts, and building community awareness through the Center for Nonprofit Excellence.

In July 2026, the University of Florida Literacy Institute (UFLI) expanded coaching and instructional support for K-3 teachers at four ACPS School Improvement sites. The collaborative is also creating a 20-member Community Advisory Council to help guide the work.

“Literacy is much more than the ability to read and write, literacy is the foundation of all opportunity, self-expression and civic engagement,” said council member E. Stanley Richardson. “As a poet, educator, and arts advocate, I have seen firsthand how literacy empowers individuals to find their voice, tell their stories and participate fully in their communities."

This fall, the Literacy Catalyst operated by PEAK Literacy will expand to serve more than 600 youth and adults with individualized tutoring across the county through virtual and community-based programs. In spring 2027, Phase Two will begin, with UFLI and additional partners working in early learning centers to expand school readiness, engaging more public schools, and expanding instructional support.

“Literacy begins long before a child enters kindergarten. Reading is more than recognizing words; comprehension gives children the power to think critically, solve problems, and shape their own futures,” said Early Learning Coalition CEO Xaviera White. “I am hopeful because Alachua County Reads is bringing families, educators, businesses and community organizations together around a shared commitment to our children. I challenge every member of our community to find a place in this effort so that every child is ready for school, ready for life and equipped to thrive.”

[See more resources available](https://alachuacounty.us/Depts/Communications/Documents/ADACompliant/ACRResources.pdf).

[Apply to join the Community Advisory Council](https://alachuacounty.us/News/Article/Pages/Alachua-County-Reads-Collaborative-Literacy-Initiative-Takes-Big-Steps-Forward.aspx#).

For more information, contact Heidi Keegan at 941-323-5936 or [hkeegan@alachuacountyreads.org](mailto:hkeegan@alachuacountyreads.org).

![](https://i0.wp.com/gazettenet.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/MassCenterfortheBook-hg-Jacobi-08032026-01-scaled.jpg?fit=1200%2C802&ssl=1)Massachusetts Center for the Book Executive Director Courtney Andree at the nonprofit's new location at Riverside Industries in Easthampton on Monday. The nonprofit, whose mission is to promote literacy statewide, had been located in downtown Northampton since 2021. "The Massachusetts Center for the Book is one of the largest centers for the book in the country," said Andree, DANIEL JACOBI II / Staff Photo

EASTHAMPTON — The Massachusetts Center for the Book is keeping its rich history of promoting literacy across the commonwealth right here in the Pioneer Valley where it started, making a short move this summer from Northampton to Easthampton.

With a new location come new opportunities, the center’s Executive Director Courtney Andree said in an interview Monday inside the new location, studio 307 in the Cottage Street Studios. The center will continue to unpack into the currently empty space over the coming weeks, but Andree said there has already been a warm welcome.

“There’s energy here,” Andree said about Easthampton. “It’s been so welcoming so far.”

The new studio, located straight through the One Cottage Street building’s front entrance and up the first set of stairs on visitors’ left, offers more affordability and accessibility than the previous location in downtown Northampton at the D.A. Sullivan building on New South Street, Andree said.

![](https://i0.wp.com/gazettenet.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/MassCenterfortheBook-hg-Jacobi-08032026-03-1024x683.jpg?ssl=1)

![](https://i0.wp.com/gazettenet.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/MassCenterfortheBook-hg-Jacobi-08032026-05-1024x683.jpg?ssl=1)

[The Massachusetts Center for the Book](https://www.massbook.org/), a nonprofit founded in western Massachusetts in 2000, is one of 56 centers chartered by the federal Center for the Book through the Library of Congress, with locations in every state, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Marianas.

While the center hosts several statewide programs each year, Andree said it plans to launch a number of local, community activities such as readings and lessons in its new Cottage Street spot.

“The Massachusetts Center for the Book is one of the largest centers for the book in the country,” said Andree, noting that each center looks a bit different.

Andree has been the center’s executive director since 2023. The center had been located in Northampton since 2021, returning to the Valley after a stint in Boston on the Simmons University Campus.

![](https://i0.wp.com/gazettenet.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/MassCenterfortheBook-hg-Jacobi-08032026-04.jpg?resize=780%2C609&ssl=1)Massachusetts Center for the Book Executive Director Courtney Andree at the nonprofit’s new location at Riverside Industries in Easthampton on Monday. The nonprofit, whose mission is to promote literacy statewide, had been located in downtown Northampton since 2021. DANIEL JACOBI II / Staff Photo

In Easthampton, Andree said the center has already made “fantastic” connections with the Easthampton Public Library and Easthampton City Arts (ECA), a city organization that drives art production. Andree hopes to incorporate the center in the monthly ECA Art Walk, an art show with various locations around the city, and to revive the Easthampton Book Fest, which ended during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

Statewide, the center hosts a reading challenge which invites participants to read a book with a specific category each month and submit a review for rewards. Andree said the center’s oldest and most anticipated program each year, the Mass Book Awards, receives upward of 500 submissions annually for writers to be recognized across seven categories. Other programs include Letters About Literature, which participants can win money from for submitting letters, Great Reads from Great Places and more.

“We really exist to promote and support the cause of books, connect libraries and develop statewide programming that supports literacy and the literary community,” Andree said.

Some more recent initiatives includes a statewide directory where writers can create a profile to boost connection between authors, which Andree said started this summer.

This is also the third year the center has hosted the [Kids Lit Fest](https://gazettenet.com/2026/05/01/a-great-way-to-discover-new-books-kids-lit-fest-celebrates-reading-with-events-across-western-mass/), a festival that aims to spark a reading passion for children across the four counties of western Massachusetts.

“We’re really trying to reach rural areas and gateway cities with live author programming and school visits,” Andree said about the festival. “We’re bringing authors into schools and kind of boosting excitement around books at a time when that’s dwindling for our kids.”

Andree said declining readership for books and novels is a challenge right now for all ages. According to Massachusetts Comprehensive Assessment System (MCAS) data, in 2025, 7% of students across grades 3-8 exceeded expectations in English Language Arts (ELA), and only 34% of students met expectations. Eight years ago, in 2017, the number of students statewide exceeding expectations was 10%, and 42% of students met expectations.

To boost reading and literacy among kids, Andree said developing the skills need to start as early as possible in schools and homes.

“It’s a pattern that needs to happen in your household, and it needs to be something that’s familywide,” she said. “That’s something that we’re trying to tackle.”

The center collaborates with libraries across the state sharing similar goals, [recently advocating for increased funding](https://gazettenet.com/2026/01/18/western-mass-libraries-advocacy/) for libraries. Andree said the center receives funding from the state, donations, private grants and other sources, but not federal funding.

The center is currently piloting a program called [Gateways to Reading](https://www.massbook.org/gateways), partnering with local WIC (Women, Infant and Children) providers and the Valley Opportunity Council to run an early literacy program which provides age-appropriate books to children at doctor visits.

“You need to read together as a family and you need to see your parents reading if you’re going to become a reader,” Andree said.

Andree said screens like cellphones and TVs are part of the decline in reading, but there are many things competing for people’s attention now. She said many schools have shifted to teaching ELA (English Language Arts) on laptops and tablets, starting at an early age.

“Some kids will graduate high school without having read a full-length novel,” Andree said.

But reading doesn’t need to always happen with physical media, Andree said, advocating for the consumption of literature through audiobooks, virtually and other ways. It’s important to support writers and authors in any way possible, Andree said, adding that there will always be a strong contingency of readers and literature lovers.

“There are fearless people fighting to get books into people’s hands every day,” she said. “We have to keep trying, and we have.”

For more information, visit [massbook.org](https://www.massbook.org/).

# 2026 TEACH Grants bring engineering, arts and literacy projects to Marion-area schools

Teachers across Marion and Morrow counties received $38,000 in 2026 TEACH Grants from Marion Community Foundation to fund innovative classroom projects benefiting students across multiple grade levels.

By Marion Community Foundation

Press Release

August 5, 2026 8:47 am

MARION, OH ( [MARION COUNTY NOW](http://www.marioncountynow.com/ ""))— Before students fill classrooms this fall, teachers across Marion and Morrow counties have been busy imagining new ways to inspire them. Thanks to Marion Community Foundation’s 2026 TEACH Grants, many of those ideas are about to become reality.

The Foundation recently awarded $38,000 through its TEACH — Teaching, Educating And Classroom Help – Grants Program to 21 teachers representing nearly every school district in Marion and Morrow counties. As the 2026-27 academic year is about to start, the recipient teachers are prepared to launch their programs. The annual TEACH Grants program has provided educators with funding for creative classroom projects that go beyond what traditional school budgets can support.

From literacy initiatives and music to engineering, fine arts, life skills programs, and innovative technology, this year’s grants reflect the creativity and dedication of local educators—and the generosity of community donors.

“TEACH grants are a way Marion Community Foundation and its donors are investing directly in local students,” said Kate McCleese, program manager at Marion Community Foundation. “Teachers know what inspires their students and what opportunities would make the biggest difference. This program gives classroom teachers the resources to bring those ideas to life.”

The grants will fund a variety of experiences. Projects include expanded engineering opportunities, 3D digital sculpting, outdoor learning spaces, performing arts programs, school library expansion, support for special education classrooms, and hands-on learning experiences in entrepreneurship, agriculture, photography, and financial literacy.

The TEACH Grants Program is made possible through support from the Dennis & Sara Trachsel Foundation and several charitable funds held at Marion Community Foundation, including the Pillar Credit Union Teachers’ Fund, Pillar Credit Union Morrow County Teachers’ Fund, and Ray & Charlotte Baldauf Fund. School-specific support also comes from the Allen ‘Bus’ Augenstein Teachers Fund, Brown Family Teachers Fund, Marion Education Foundation Fund, and River Valley Teachers Fund.

“Many people think of scholarships when they think about supporting education,” said Julie Prettyman, Foundation President & CEO. “TEACH grants are another meaningful way donors can make a difference. They empower teachers to create memorable learning experiences that can spark curiosity, build confidence, and impact students for years to come.”

The 2026 TEACH Grants support projects at Elgin, Marion City, Pleasant, River Valley, St. Mary, Highland, and Mt. Gilead schools, benefiting students from kindergarten through high school across a wide range of academic subjects and enrichment opportunities.

A complete list of 2026 TEACH Grant recipients and funded projects follows:

**Elgin Local Schools**

**Elgin Middle School \| Andrea Coykendall \| Life Skills Classroom** This grant will support life skills instruction for students in a new cross-categorical special education classroom by providing materials for cooking, cleaning, budgeting and other hands-on activities.

**Marion City Schools**

**Harding High School \| Adam Hanke \| Elevating Our Art** This grant will enhance drawing and painting instruction by using professional-quality art supplies, presentation materials for student artwork and opportunities for extracurricular art experiences.

**Harding High School \| Jacob Hartman \| Multi-Ensemble Digital Piano Upgrade for Marion City Schools Band Programs**

This grant will replace a failing digital piano system used by marching band, jazz ensembles, indoor percussion, solo performances and other music programs, ensuring students have quality equipment for instruction and performance.

**Harding High School \| Jami Rawlins \| Harding Singers Lighting and Performance Project**

This grant will purchase wireless, computer-programmed lighting and other performance equipment to enhance productions by the Harding Singers, a competitive show choir that performs throughout the region and hosts an annual competition.

**Grant Middle School \| Aaron Edwards \| Engineering**

This grant will expand engineering projects by providing materials for soldering electrical components, woodworking and other hands-on learning experiences.

**Grant Middle School \| Jessica Clarke \| VOX Books**

This grant will purchase VOX Books, which feature built-in audio narration in multiple languages and reading levels, helping engage young readers while supporting struggling readers and English language learners.

**Garfield Elementary School \| Lily Janson \| Specialized Learning Center**

This grant will purchase sensory equipment for a specialized learning center classroom, helping students with disabilities develop sensory, social and emotional regulation skills while increasing independence and readiness to learn.

**Pleasant Local Schools**

**Pleasant High School \| Kirsten Jordan \| CCP Photography Course**

This grant will support a College Credit Plus photography course in coordination with Columbus State, providing students with instruction in studio and digital photography, portfolio development and career exploration.

**Pleasant High School \| Paula Ritter \| It’s a Zoo Here! — Enriching a Zoology Course**

This grant will purchase zoological specimens, microscope slides, display charts and tissue samples to provide students with hands-on learning opportunities in zoology.

**River Valley Local Schools**

**River Valley Middle School \| Laura Carey \| Pixels to Polymers**

This grant will expand the school’s digital art program by introducing 3D digital sculpting and additive manufacturing, allowing students to transform digital designs into physical creations.

**Liberty Elementary \| Samantha Coyan \| Audio Adventures**

This grant will purchase VOX Books for kindergarten students, combining print books with built-in audio narration to strengthen early literacy skills, build confidence and encourage independent reading.

**Heritage Elementary \| Laura Rengert \| The Book Drop**

This grant will create a pseudo book vending machine that rewards students with age-appropriate books, encouraging literacy and helping build home libraries.

**St. Mary School**

**St. Mary School \| Library Enrichment**

This grant will purchase a library management system and support subscriptions to digital resources, improving access to library materials for students.

**Highland Local Schools**

**Highland Elementary \| Dirk Detillion \| Greenhouse**

This student-led project will provide hands-on learning in agriculture, entrepreneurship and sustainability as students grow, care for and sell plants while developing teamwork, responsibility and business skills.

**Highland Elementary \| Samantha Johnson \| Cultivating Curiosity Outside the Classroom**

This grant will create an outdoor learning space where students explore science, teamwork and responsibility through gardening and hands-on learning experiences.

**Highland Elementary \| Madison Craigo \| Kindness Club**

This student-led club will encourage fifth-grade students to plan and lead projects that promote kindness, school beautification, service and encouragement throughout the school.

**Highland High School \| Craig Smith \| Sustaining Personalized Strength & Conditioning Through Performance Tracking Technology**

This grant will support strength and conditioning software that provides individualized workouts and performance tracking while helping students develop goal-setting, data analysis and lifelong fitness habits.

**Highland Elementary \| Kayla Arthurs \| Instruments for the Elementary Music Classroom**

This grant will purchase additional musical instruments, including African gourds, maracas, hand drums and rhythm sticks, allowing more K-5 students to participate in hands-on music instruction.

**Mt. Gilead Local Schools**

**Park Avenue Elementary \| Mackenzie Hoffman \| The Park Avenue Student Market**

This grant will support a student-run marketplace where students apply math concepts such as budgeting, fractions, decimals, measurement and data analysis while building financial literacy, collaboration and problem-solving skills.

**Mt. Gilead High School \| Hanna Vanderkooi \| Rise and Shine Cafe**

This grant will support a student-run coffee shop where entrepreneurship students gain hands-on experience in business operations, marketing, finance, technology and customer service.

**Mt. Gilead High School \| Tom Lewis \| T-shirt Press Room Storage & Rack System**

This grant will purchase modular storage and organization systems for the school’s student-run direct-to-film printing operation, improving workflow and creating a more professional production environment.

Springfield Public Schools is honing in on literacy at key grade levels with its new 417 Reads initiative this school year. Superintendent Grenita Lathan announced the program during her annual State of the Schools speech Thursday, Aug. 6.

Community movers and shakers gathered for the Springfield Area Chamber of Commerce’s monthly Good Morning, Springfield! networking breakfast in the new gymnasium at [Pipkin Middle School](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/pipkin-middle-school-construction-update/), which is officially opening for students later this month. Many attendees were eager to support students in the new reading program.

Lathan said that 69% of fourth-grade students in the U.S. are reading below grade level and two-thirds of students who cannot read proficiently by the end of fourth grade will “end up in jail or on welfare.”

“These numbers are staggering and highlight the reason we focus on literacy as a key priority at SPS,” Lathan said.

![](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/080626_pipkin_EF_028.jpg?resize=780%2C487&ssl=1)The big announcement during Superintendent Lathan’s speech was 417 Reads, a literacy program started by the school district. (Photo by Ellie Frysztak)

417 Reads will impact 1,600 SPS third graders in the 2026-27 school year if 75 people volunteer to be mentors through the program, Lathan said. She later announced that over 110 people at Good Morning, Springfield! had filled out volunteer interest forms on the spot.

Mentors with 417 Reads will read aloud to third-grade students once every month during the school year. Students will also receive sturdy boxes for books that can become small take-home libraries. The program, which is in partnership with [Scholastic](https://education.scholastic.com/education/programs/scholastic-real.html), may be expanded to serve fourth-grade students if the district receives support from enough volunteers, Lathan said.

## Two new schools opening up this month

![](https://i0.wp.com/sgfcitizen.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_4856.jpg?resize=780%2C466&ssl=1)Pipkin students gather inside the library at the new Pipkin Middle School on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Ellie Frysztak)

In addition to Pipkin Middle, SPS is opening up another brand-new facility for the 2026-27 year: [Reed Academy](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/athletic-center-lafayette-park/). The district is also getting started on a few other construction projects funded by the Proposition S that [passed with strong support](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/220-million-school-bond-measure-has-overwhelming-early-support/) from voters in 2023.

SPS broke ground on two construction projects this summer for the new Bissett Elementary and Pershing Middle schools, and at 5:30 p.m. on Aug. 6 SPS will break ground on the new Bingham Elementary, marking the final construction project in a $220 million [bond package](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/bissett-pershing-bingham-groundbreaking/) approved by voters in 2023.

Lathan said SPS is keeping its promises by “transforming our district learning environment and achieving it on time and on budget” thanks to residents’ ongoing support of Proposition S.

In addition to the emphasis on literacy with 417 Reads, Lathan shared five other focus areas the district will prioritize in the 2026-27 school year:

- Customer service for SPS parents, students and other community members
- Opportunity expansion through more transportation opportunities and new “outdoor pursuits” for students
- Digital citizenship, with a new comprehensive technology plan that will “set a clear roadmap” for digital tools, AI and academic integrity in the classroom
- A facility master plan update, which will look ahead to the next decade
- Academics and workforce readiness programs, incuding partnershisps with local businesses

## SPS touts ‘opportunity expansion’

Lathan said transportation expansion is part of the district’s focus on opportunities for students this year. SPS [began a three-year plan](https://sgfcitizen.org/schools/k12-education/sps-expanding-school-bus-eligibility-over-next-three-years/) in 2025 to make its school bus system more efficient and responsive.

“We’re further expanding our school busing capabilities so more students have reliable, safe access to specialized programs. … Removing transportation barriers for students who attend Choice programs is one more example of how SPS opens doors to opportunities,” Lathan said.

The superintendent also highlighted the [Outdoor Pursuits](https://www.sps.org/academics-programs/choice-programs/outdoor-pursuits) program, a semester-long opportunity launching in August for high school juniors and seniors. Participants from all five SPS high schools will be able to learn outdoors skills and potentially earn credentials, including safety-related certifications and hunting or fishing licenses.

“Through expanding access and visionary programs like Outdoor Pursuits, we’re redefining what public education can look like one student, one choice and one opportunity at a time,” Lathan said.

In the summer of 1944, Allied forces were fighting some of their fiercest or most daring battles, while also reaping some of their most auspicious victories. On June 5, Allied troops entered Rome in the afternoon, and it became the first capital of the Axis Powers to fall. Meanwhile in Normandy, the following day, June 6, was D-Day, the amphibious landing of troops in northern France, opening the Western Front. In July, the Allies pushed inland. In the sweltering summer days of August-September 1944, Allied infantry troops won the bloody battle for the port of Brest in Brittany, and in another amphibious landing in France, the major ports of Marseille and Toulon were reclaimed, easing the Allies’ supply crisis. Meanwhile in the Pacific Theater, Saipan fell in June after a fearsome banzai charge; a decisive clash of carriers in the Philippine Sea crippled Japanese air power, and by August, Guam was recaptured.

In the summer of 1944 at Barksdale Army Air Field, as Barksdale was known prior to the creation of the United States Air Force on September 18, 1947, 35 or more enlisted men were fighting a brave battle of their own, proving they had the basic readiness to be soldiers by attending what the air field newspaper called “elementary school for soldiers who can neither read nor write.” At that time, one of Barksdale’s missions was as to serve as one of the Army Air Corps “replacement training centers”. These centers provided training for newly-enlisted Air Corps soldiers that was not yet specialized for a specific assignment.

Earlier in 1944, President Roosevelt had declared the US Army and Navy were faced with a “grave manpower shortage,” desperately in need of more able-bodied combat replacements. To help meet that shortage, Roosevelt asked the selective service (“the draft”) to revisit service deferments, whether for occupational, dependency, age, or physical or mental fitness requirements. For the same purpose, Chairman Andrew J. May of the U.S. House Military Affairs Committee argued that among other reclassifications, the army “should quit rejecting men because of illiteracy. Men who are illiterate can still be sharpshooters.”

In January of that year, Major Isaac N. Carr, preinduction officer of the Army’s 4th Service Command headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia, announced in a speech to junior college officials, that was covered by the Associated Press, that the United States had 341,000 physically fit men of service age who were functionally illiterate, meaning, at that time, that their reading and writing skills were at a fourth-grade level or below. Carr illustrated this number by saying that was enough physically-able men to make up more than 20 Army divisions.

If the number 341,000 for men whose only barrier to service at that moment was that they read at a fourth-grade (or below) level sounds inordinately high, keep in mind that, although all states had a compulsory education law on the books by 1918, those laws were not consistently enforced across the country until well into the 1930s. That time frame would cover the school years of WWII enlistees. In addition, quality schools and trained teachers were still not available to many African American students in the south during the school years of those enlistees. For example, a high school for African American students in Bossier City did not open until the beginning of the 1940s.

To rectify this deficiency, Army training units were called upon to provide literacy instruction. The Saturday July 1, 1944, issue of the Barksdale’s Bark newspaper announced that “an elementary school for soldiers who can neither read nor write will be started by Base S-3 \[the operations and training office\] shortly.” The article shared that 35 enlisted men had been assigned by their commanding officers to the school already, and that classes would be held 3 times a day, five days a week. Students were required to attend one of the daily sessions in the school room in the commissary building.

More details about a literacy class were announced in the Bark on Saturday, July 29, 1944. This time it said the classes would be offered in the “Kindergarten building.” This was likely the base’s brand-new preschool for children through the age of 5. The article further stated that “Commanding officers of all units are cooperating with Base S-3 in getting men to attend the classes,” and that “the latest pamphlets from the Armed Institute have been procured for instructional purposes.”

This pamphlet referred to for the literacy classes at Barksdale likely referred to Technical Manual No. 21-500, also known as the “Private Pete” books. These reading primers followed along with solider Private Pete and all that he’d likely encounter in his day-to-day life in the Army. (The Navy had their own booklets, featuring “Sailor Sam.”) These stories adhered to the same basic format and learn-to-read formula as the ubiquitous Dick and Jane readers that young children in school at the time were using. The article also named the teacher of the literacy classes, Mrs. Mary E. Laurent, wife of Lt. Harry Laurent, Jr. assistant S-1 (personnel) officer at Barksdale. Mrs. Laurent, who “offered her services as teacher of the classes,” was introduced to Bark readers as a graduate of Muskingum College in Ohio, and an experienced teacher of English. Both Laurents were from Ohio and had attended Muskingum.

Being singled out by one’s commanding officer to attend classes in a preschool building, with text books modeled after children’s readers, Dick and Jane, could sound like excruciating punishment. Many WWII veterans’ own stories of being able to “go back in time” and learn to read and write, suggest appreciation for the opportunity, however. As for the Laurents, they were married 69 years and lived around the world while Mr. Laurent was an industrial psychologist, and retired in Hendersonville, North Carolina. They continued to value access to education, by establishing a scholarship for students in Henderson County, and endowing a department chair in Psychology at their Alma Mater, Muskingum College, now University.

State Sen. Matt Brass discussed education, healthcare and growth during a visit to the White Oak Golden Kiwanis Club on Thursday.

The Newnan Republican highlighted new restrictions on student cellphone use, homeowners association reforms, a statewide literacy initiative, Medicaid policy and the debate over data centers.

Brass said he evaluates legislation by considering its effect on three generations: older Georgians, working families and children.

Nearly three-quarters of Georgia's almost $39 billion budget is devoted to education and healthcare, Brass said, calling those investments critical to all three generations.

**School cellphone ban expands to high schools**

Brass said one of the most significant education measures approved this year expands Georgia's cellphone restrictions from middle schools to high schools.

Lawmakers acted after receiving overwhelmingly positive feedback from educators following the middle school ban approved two years ago, he said.

According to Brass, teachers and administrators reported students were more engaged in class, spent more time interacting with one another and experienced fewer problems related to cyberbullying.

"We wanted to get away from that," Brass said, referring to online harassment among students. "We wanted to make sure this next generation isn't living here," he said while gesturing toward a cellphone, "and they're living more here with that face-to-face interaction."

Brass joked that his own son, who started eighth grade Thursday, asked if there was a way to repeal the law after learning it would eventually apply when he reaches high school.

"I told him he already had that ban last year in middle school, so you're going to be used to it in high school," Brass said. "He didn't like that answer."

**HOA law increases oversight**

Brass devoted much of his presentation to legislation reforming homeowners associations, calling it the most difficult bill he has handled during his legislative career.

The new law requires homeowners associations, condominium associations and property owners associations to register with the Georgia Secretary of State's Office, where governing documents, financial information and board officers will be on file.

Brass said the legislation was prompted by complaints from homeowners who struggled to obtain financial records or challenge decisions made by HOA boards.

The measure also creates a complaint process through the Secretary of State's Office. Independent hearing officers will review disputes, with appeals first going to magistrate court before reaching superior court, reducing the need for homeowners to hire attorneys.

The legislation raises the foreclosure threshold for unpaid HOA assessments from $2,000 to $4,000. Only unpaid dues and approved special assessments may count toward that amount, while attorney fees and fines for violations such as failing to mow a lawn cannot be used to trigger foreclosure.

Brass said the goal was to improve accountability, transparency and fairness while preserving associations' ability to collect legitimate dues.

**Literacy coaches**

Brass also highlighted one of the General Assembly's largest education investments this year: funding literacy coaches in every public elementary school serving students in kindergarten through third grade.

The initiative, funded at approximately $70 million, was approved through House Bill 1193, sponsored by House Education Committee Chairman Chris Erwin, R-Homer, and backed by House Speaker Jon Burns and Gov. Brian Kemp as part of a broader effort to improve Georgia's reading proficiency.

Rather than teaching students directly, the school-based and regional literacy coaches will work alongside classroom teachers, modeling instruction, providing coaching and helping schools implement evidence-based reading practices.

Brass said the effort was modeled after Mississippi's nationally recognized literacy reforms, which dramatically improved that state's reading scores over the past decade.

"It was an expensive undertaking, but I think the return on investment there is going to be tenfold," Brass said.

The program will be phased in over the next several years as coaches are hired and placed in schools across Georgia.

Brass said former Coweta Sheriff Mike Yeager and current Sheriff Lenn Wood have both pointed to third-grade reading proficiency when discussing long-term incarceration trends, arguing that students who fall behind in reading early are more likely to face problems later in life.

**Medicaid expansion**

During a question-and-answer session, Brass said Georgia continues to rely on a waiver-based Medicaid program rather than fully expanding coverage under the Affordable Care Act.

He said the state's current approach extends coverage and subsidies to some residents above traditional Medicaid eligibility while limiting Georgia's long-term financial exposure. Conservative concerns about relying on long-term federal funding were reinforced this year after enhanced federal health insurance subsidies expired, he argued, increasing pressure on states to address coverage costs.

That uncertainty, he said, is a key reason Georgia has resisted full Medicaid expansion.

At the same time, Brass acknowledged the state must confront uncompensated care, noting that hospitals ultimately shift those costs to consumers through higher healthcare and insurance prices.

“If we're not going to do ACA, we've got to do something," Brass said.

**Data centers draw questions**

Audience members also pressed Brass on the rapid growth of data centers and whether their heavy electricity use could drive up utility bills for residential customers.

Brass's comments come as Coweta County continues to debate proposed large-scale data center developments, including Project Oak.

He said current Public Service Commission rules require data centers to pay for electric infrastructure upgrades made necessary by their projects. Although legislation to permanently

write those protections into state law failed this year, Brass said he expects lawmakers to revisit the issue next session.

He also pushed back on some public concerns surrounding data centers, saying misinformation has complicated the debate.

Brass said many newer facilities are shifting to closed-loop cooling systems that recycle water instead of continually drawing new supplies.

He also argued that some high-voltage transmission line projects in west Georgia were planned to accommodate regional growth, not solely because of proposed data centers.

"There are some legitimate concerns out there, and we do need to be asking questions," Brass said. "But there's also a lot of bad information out there around data centers."
